answer: `set pm-control-entry-<resource>/<period>/<direction>/<location> tca-supervision true` arms threshold-crossing supervision on the port; data-supervision true/false arms the collection itself. `add`/`set pm-threshold-<resource>/<period>/<direction>/<location>/<parameter> low-threshold <v> high-threshold <v>` sets the limit on that instance, with parameter = errored-seconds. `pm-threshold-profile-<resource-type>/<direction>/<location>/<period>/<parameter>` holds the per-type value and exposes default-low-threshold, default-high-threshold, min-value and max-value, e.g. `set pm-threshold-profile-OTUC14i/ingress/near-end/pm-24h/errored-seconds high-threshold 1200`. pm-profile-entry carries default-tca-supervision for newly created resources. direction is ingress, egress, all or na (default all); location all, na, near-end or far-end (default all).

`add ntp-key-<key-id> key-type <sha-1|aes-cmac|sha-256|md5> key-value <value> [is-trusted true]` - key-id range 1..65534, key-value length 8..40, is-trusted default false. `add ntp-server-<ip-address> auth-key-id <n>` - IPv4, IPv6 or DNS name; origin manual (default) or dhcp; auth-key-id default not-applicable; admin-state default unlock. `set ntp ntp-enabled true ntp-auth-enabled true` - ntp-enabled defaults true, ntp-auth-enabled false, assignment-method manual, dhcp or both (default both). Verify with `show ntp-server-status-<ip>`: auth-status ok, yes, bad or none (default none), and reach, an 8-bit shift register where 377 means all recent probes were answered, plus stratum, offset, jitter and condition (sys.peer). `show ntp ntp-active-server` names the server in use and `show clock time-source` should read ntp.

`protection-switch` moves traffic, `manual-switchover` moves the controller. `protection-switch [-f] [operation-type=]<force|lockout|manual|release> [switch-target=]<value> [protection-group=]<value>`, Operational mode; switch-target is not needed for the release and lockout operations. Example: `protection-switch protection-group-test operation-type=force switch-target=protection`. The persistent equivalent is protection-group pg-request (clear default, manual-to-working, manual-to-protection, forced-to-working, forced-to-protection, protection-lockout, exercise). `manual-switchover [-f] [resource=]<AID>` takes a card AID, e.g. `manual-switchover card-1-3`, and prompts: Controller will switchover and connection to the management interface will be lost.

`set-time` is only applicable when time-source is manual, that is when NTP is not enabled, which is what rejects it. `show clock` gives time-source (ntp or manual, default manual), current-time, universal-time, timezone, DST-active and last-time-jump (jumps of less than 10 seconds are ignored). If it reads ntp, check `show ntp ntp-enabled` and `show ntp-server-status-<ip>` for reach (377 = all probes answered), offset and condition. To set it by hand, `set ntp ntp-enabled false`, then `set-time 2021-02-06T11:16:58Z` - ISO 8601 combined date and time, Z for UTC or +/-hh:mm for another zone. `time` prints the current time using the system-configured timezone, not the one given to set-time. Timezone is `set clock timezone <value>`, default Universal-Time-Coordinated.

`show ne` identifies the node: ne-id, ne-name (default '1830 GX'), ne-type (G30 or G40), node-type (ILA, OADM, XPDR), ne-site, ne-location, clli, node-controller-chassis-name (default 1), recover-mode. `status`, or `status system`, is the dashboard: name/id/type, active and inactive SW labels, uptime, management IP, alarm counts per severity and an equipment summary; `status equipment [chassis-id]` trees chassis, cards and toms. `show slot` gives supported-type versus installed-type per position. The cost: `restart [-h] [-f] [<resource-id>] [<type>] [<sub-component>]`. With no resource-id the active controller card restarts; with no type a warm restart is done. cold reboots all components and is service affecting, connectivity back within five minutes; warm reboots the processor and is non service affecting; shutdown gracefully shuts the card down. Confirmation is required unless -f.

The occupant is `card-1-2` (card-<name>, keyed by chassis-name and slot-name). Beneath a card hang comm-eth, inventory, port, property, sub-component, tom and usb; beneath each port hang current-fw, serdes and supported-tom-power. The holder `slot-1-2` also carries current-fw and reports supported-type, installed-type, oper-state, avail-state and current-equipment. The pluggable is `tom-<card-name>-<port-name>`, e.g. tom-1-2-T1, with required-type CFP2-DCO, OSFP, QSFP28, QSFPDD, QSFPDD-ZR, QSFPPLUS, SFP or SFPPLUS. Its FRU inventory is read with `show inventory-<card-name>-<port-name>`, e.g. `show inventory-1-3-1`: hardware-version, actual-type, actual-subtype, PON, serial-number, clei, vendor, part-number, manufacture-date, insertion-date, number-of-lanes, vendor-compliance-code, actual-power-class (1..8), actual-max-power-draw and fw-status.

Model capability comes from the show-only supported-* family. `show supported-card-<card-type>` gives node-type-compatibility (all, ILA, OADM), supported-subtype, default-card-mode and supported-card-mode, card-width (na, single-slot, double-slot, half-slot, triple-slot), card-height in RUs, is-field-replaceable, category, grid-mode-support, max-power-draw, leds, location-led-support, console-port-support, support-serdes-config, supported-bands and supported-features. Per port, `show supported-port-<card-type>/<port-name>` gives port-type, direction, configuration-mode, faceplate-label, default-tom and allows-auto-migration; also supported-slot, supported-chassis, supported-tom and tom-type. What the installed unit is doing is `show card-<name>`: required-type, required-subtype, card-mode, category, chassis-name, slot-name, power-profile, max-power-draw, last-reboot-reason, admin-state, oper-state, avail-state.

Instance, then area, then interface, then the neighbor appears. `add ospf-instance-<instance-id> router-id <dotted-quad>` - instance-id 0..255, version ospfv2 (default) or ospfv3, router-id-mode manual or use-loopback (default use-loopback); with use-loopback an ipv4 LO-MGMT address must be configured. `add ospf-area-<instance-id>/<ospf-area-id>` - the OSPF instance must be created before the area. `add ospf-interface-<instance-id>/<ospf-area-id>/<ospf-if-name>` - instance and area must be present; ospf-if-name is a leafref to an existing interface if-name; enable default true, hello-interval default 10 (1..32767 s), router-dead-interval default 40 (4..65535 s), ospf-cost default 10, priority default 1. `show ospf-neighbor-<instance-id>/<area-id>/<if-name>/<router-id>` shows how far it got: state down, init, 2-way, exstart, exchange, loading or full, and role drother, dr, bdr or ptp. Both NEs must have instance, area and interface and be connected with DCN interface bridges; the neighbor is deleted when the OSPF interface is down.

`show software-load-<location-id>/<swload-state>` is the per-card view, e.g. `show software-load-1-5/active`; swload-state is active, inactive or installable. It reports swload-version, swload-manifest, swload-prepared, swload-status (validate/apply/activate/cancel in-progress, complete, failed or timeout), swload-activation-type (direct, warmstart, coldstart), swload-vendor, swload-product, swload-label and swload-pkg-type. The pieces are `show sw-component-<location-id>/<swload-state>/<name>` with state installed, not-installed, installation-failed or unknown, plus version and description, and one level deeper `show sw-subcomponent-<location-id>/<swload-state>/<sw-component-name>/<sw-subcomponent-name>`. The bundled firmware is `show packaged-fw-<location-id>/<swload-state>/<equipment-type>/<fw-name> fw-version`, and versions of the same firmware differ per equipment-type.

`show lldp-port-statistics-<lldp-port>/ingress` answers it: total-frames-out is what you transmit, total-frames-in what you receive, and error-frames, total-discarded-frames, total-discarded-tlvs, total-unrecognized-tlvs and total-ageouts show what is being thrown away; all default 0, bounded by last-change-time and last-clear-time. Counters for a port freeze whenever lldp-admin-status is disabled on that port, and the egress direction is not supported. `show lldp-neighbor-<lldp-port>/ingress` shows what was learned (chassis-id, port-id, system-name, ttl, age, last-update) and is kept indefinitely until the port is decommissioned or cleared. `show lldp-local-info-<lldp-port>` shows what you advertise: chassis-id is the chassis serial number, port-id the port AID, system-name the NE name. `show lldp hold-on-timer` defaults to 900 seconds and applies when a neighbor sends no TTL TLV.

`show slot-<chassis-name>-<slot-name>`, or `show slot` for all positions, gives AID, supported-type, installed-type, oper-state, avail-state and current-equipment, so an empty installed-type against a populated supported-type is a vacant slot. FRU detail for the occupant is `show inventory-<chassis-name>-<slot-name>`: hardware-version, actual-type, actual-subtype, sw-support-revision, PON, serial-number, clei, vendor, part-number, manufacture-date, insertion-date and fw-status (not-applicable, current, not-current or unavailable). Firmware level is `show current-fw-<chassis-name>-<slot-name>/<fw-name>`, also addressable as current-fw-<card-name>-<port-name>/<fw-name>, returning fw-version, expected-fw-version and fw-status current, not-current or unavailable (default unavailable). `show equipment` and `status equipment` give the rolled-up view.

`show manifest-<manifest-file>` gives manifest-signature, downloaded-on and information. The contents split two ways: `show manifest-component-<manifest-file>/<equipment-type>/<name> [state] [version] [description]`, where state is installed, not-installed, installation-failed or unknown (default unknown), and `show manifest-firmware-<manifest-file>/<equipment-type>/<fw-name> [fw-version]` for the firmware carried in it. `show fru-info-<manifest-file>/<equipment-type>` displays the packaged FRU information for one equipment-type, and `show downloaded-image-<manifest-file>/<name> [signature]` covers the image files. For progress rather than per-package state, `show upgrade-status-<resource>` reports at ne, chassis or card level with to-swload-version, status, start-time, end-time, step and details.

Alarm severity defaults sit in alarm-severity-profile, whose rows are alarm-severity-entry-<resource-type>/<alarm-type>/<direction>/<location>, e.g. `set alarm-severity-entry-OTU2/TIM/ingress/near-end severity minor`. Severities are critical, event, major, minor, not-reported and warning; direction na, ingress or egress; location na, near-end or far-end; show also exposes service-affecting (indeterminate, sa, nsa, sa-nsa). Both objects are system-managed and cannot be manually deleted. PM defaults come from pm-profile-entry-<resource-type>/<direction>/<location>/<period>, whose default-data-supervision and default-tca-supervision decide, for newly created resources of that type, whether data supervision and threshold-crossing supervision start enabled. Default limits per type are in pm-threshold-profile (default-low-threshold, default-high-threshold, min-value, max-value), and pm-profile global-data-supervision is auto-enabled or manual (default manual).

The decision is ipsec-spd-entry-<ikev2-local-instance-name>/<ikev2-peer-name>/<ipsec-spd-entry-name>. Its action is protect, bypass or discard (default protect), and priority (uint8, mandatory on add) gives precedence between SPD entries. Other attributes: ipsec-protocol ESP, mode tunnel (default) or transport, esn default true, anti-replay-window 32..1024 default 64 when action is protect, dynamic-ts default disabled. Beneath it hang ipsec-sa-proposal and ipsec-traffic-selector (next-layer-protocol any = 0, opaque = 255, or a number 0-255, default any); beneath the traffic selector hang local-subnet and remote-subnet, keyed by prefix, and local-ports and remote-ports, keyed by start and stop. The SPD entry sits under ikev2-peer, which sits under ikev2-local-instance. Example: `add ipsec-spd-entry-ipsec/GX2/dns priority 1 action protect`.

trusted-certificate is the CA you trust: the X509v3 root and intermediate certificates trusted by the system, and what every other certificate's trust-chain points at. local-certificate is this node's own X.509v3 end-entity certificate representing one of the secure application identities; it uniquely carries used-by, self-signed and subject-alternative-names. peer-certificate is the far end: the X509v3 end-entity certificate representing a trusted remote peer for the L1 encryption secure application, with the extra white-listed attribute meaning it was imported without a trust chain. certificate is not a holder at all but the action command - `show certificates`, `show certificate-revocation`, `clear certificate type=<trusted|local|peer> id=<id>`. All three share version v3, serial-number, subject-name, issuer, valid-from, valid-to, status, public-key-length (rsa2048/3072/4096, ecdsa256/384/521) and revocation-mode auto, force-revoked or force-unrevoked (default auto).

Import with `import-certificate {-i, <certificate type>} [<certificate-name>] <string in PEM format> [<passphrase>]`, Operational mode, PEM format. The type is local-certificate, peer-certificate or trusted-certificate, e.g. `import-certificate trusted-certificate certificate-name=trusted-cert-1 <string in PEM format>`. -i also imports the intermediate certificates in a bundle, or those named by the AIA extension of a single-certificate file; root certificates must be installed individually. Without a certificate-name the name is derived from the topmost certificate issuer /CN plus a numeric suffix. passphrase applies to trusted-certificate, local-certificate and bundles. Material can also be created locally with cert-gen (self-signed, days default 365, auto-install default true) or csr-gen, which leaves a local-certificate in pending-import state. Removal is `clear [-f] certificate [type=]<trusted|local|peer> [id=]<id>`; the id must match a currently installed but unused certificate, and purge-all-invalid, purge-all-unused, purge-all-expired, purge-local-unused and purge-peer-unused are accepted in place of a type.

access-rule permits or denies: `add access-rule-<access-rule-list-name>/<access-rule-name> action <permit|deny>`, with action mandatory on add and filters path (default *), module-name (default *), attribute, attribute-value and operation (create, read, update, delete, execute; default *). access-rule-list fixes the evaluation order: it groups access-rules by user-group and is processed in order as given by sequence-id, lower ids first. sw-control-rule has nothing to do with traffic - it overrides the default action on software service failure, with fail-action default-action, ignore or system-restart. IP packet filtering itself is acl (type IPv4 or IPv6, interface 1-AUX-1, 1-AUX-2, DCN, DCN-B, DCN-2, DCN-2-B) and its ace entries, whose action is drop (default), accept or reject.

Order is set by sequence-id: the access-rule-list is processed in order as given by sequence-id, and within it lower number ids are processed first, so the lower sequence-id wins. sequence-id is a uint16 on both access-rule and access-rule-list and can be changed over the lifetime of the list to re-sort entries; if not provided it is set to the currently used latest id plus 1, so the rule goes to the end of the list. The system supports a maximum of 500 access-rules across all access-rule-lists. The access-rule-list user-group attribute is a leaf-list of user-group names whose default '*' matches all existing user-groups, and a maximum of 20 user-groups can be referenced. Example: `add access-rule-list-A user-group XY`.

It is not in snmp-community: the trap-community-string is located in the snmp-target object. Set it there with `add snmp-target-<target-name> snmpv3-user <value> target-address <value> [trap-community-string <value>]` or `set snmp-target-<target-name> trap-community-string <value>`. trap-community-string is a string of length 0..32 and defaults to infinera, which is what a receiver expecting something else rejects. Other snmp-target attributes: enabled default true, snmp-version v2c (default) or v3, snmpv3-user only when snmp-version is v3, target-port default 162 (range 0..65535), target-transport udp. snmp-community-<name>, with community-string of length 1..32 and community-string-access read-only, governs polling access rather than traps. Globally, `set snmp enabled true port 161`.

external-fiber-connection is the one written for you: it is set autonomously by TNMS, and although it can be configured manually that is not recommended. It represents the physical link between two ports of L0 cards in different NEs, or in the same NE in disaggregated configurations. Attributes: src-node-id, src-card-name, src-port-name, dst-node-id, dst-card-name, dst-port-name, label, fiber-connection-type one-way or two-way (default two-way), and scope general-purpose or cable-id (default general-purpose) - if scope is not cable-id, CableID verification excludes that connection from the CableID path. By contrast fiber-connection is user-provisioned and links two distinct ports or sub-ports within the same NE, and supporting-fiber-connection is show-only, listing the fiber-connection-list path.

Use ipv4-address: `add ipv4-address-<if-name>/<ip> netmask <value>`, for example `add ipv4-address-DCN-B/10.220.192.213 netmask 255.255.252.0`; show adds origin static (default), dhcp or auto-config. Addresses beginning with 0, with 127, or in 224 through 255 are disallowed and only valid netmasks are accepted, and a static IPv4 address cannot be configured when DHCP is enabled on the interface. The two look-alikes are read-only LLDP data, not configuration: management-address-<lldp-port>/<direction>/<address-subtype>/<address> reports the management addresses advertised by a remote system as received on a local port, and management-address-local-<lldp-port>/<address-subtype>/<address> reports those this node advertises. Both only expose if-subtype (unknown, if-index, system-port-number), if-id and address-oid.

The stated pre-condition on ipv4-address is that a static IPv4 address cannot be configured when DHCP is enabled on the interface, which is the usual refusal. Check `show interface-<if-name> ipv4-address-assignment-method` - static (default) or dhcp - and ipv4-enabled (default true), and switch it with `set interface-<if-name> ipv4-address-assignment-method static`. The address must also be legal: addresses beginning with 0, with 127, or in 224 through 255 are disallowed, and only valid netmasks may be configured. To see which interfaces exist, press ? after `ipv4-address-` for the object completion options, or run `show interface`, which lists if-type (ethernet, software-loopback, point-to-point, ppp, hdlc), supporting-port, admin-state and oper-state. `show ipv4-address-<if-name>/<ip> origin` reveals whether an existing address is static, dhcp or auto-config.

Everything in use is under route: `show route-<rib-name>/<destination-prefix>` lists system routes from all sources and reports source-protocol (OSPF, BGP, static and so on) plus special-next-hop none (default), blackhole or unreachable. Routes live in RIBs - `show rib-<rib-name> [vrf] [address-family]`, address-family ipv4-unicast or ipv6-unicast, one system-controlled default RIB per address family per routing instance - and resolved hops are `show next-hop-<rib-name>/<destination-prefix>/<interface>`, e.g. `show next-hop-IPv4/0.0.0.0/0/DCN`. Hand-typed routes are added with `add ipv4-static-route-<ipv4-destination-prefix>/<vrf> [next-hop-address <v>] [advertised <true|false>] [distance <1..255>] [interface <v>] [origin <manual|dhcp>] [special-next-hop blackhole]`; advertised defaults false, distance 1, origin manual. ipv6-static-route is the IPv6 equivalent.

local-ports and remote-ports belong to the security tunnel. Both are keyed <ikev2-local-instance-name>/<ikev2-peer-name>/<ipsec-spd-entry-name>/<ipsec-traffic-selector-name>/<start>/<stop> and nest under ipsec-traffic-selector, supporting only add, show and delete. start takes all, opaque or a port number; stop is a port number defaulting to 0, and 0 is accepted only when start is all or opaque. Examples: `add local-ports-ipsec/GX1/dns/ts1/53/53`, `add remote-ports-ipsec/GX2/protect1/ts1/all`. connection-ports is the connectivity one: `show connection-ports-<degree-number>/<index> [port-name]`, show-only, nested under a degree. degree-number is 1..20 and must not exceed max-degrees; index has range 1..2 but is always 1 in the 1830 GX because dwdm-line ports are bidirectional; port-name is the dwdm-line port of an RD or ILAx card.

`take-snapshot [[db-passphrase=]<value>] [[db-instance=]<value>] [[description=]<value>]` makes the copy, Operational mode. db-instance is temp (default, temporary storage for manual backup and restore), manual (permanent), or the automatic onehour, oneday, oneweek, plus rollback; type is db-backup (default) or system-backup; description up to 128 characters. Re-taking an existing instance overwrites it. It is refused unless the db-passphrase used for snapshot encryption is configured, either globally in security-policies or as a parameter here: minimum 40 characters, no dictionary words, characters from the 85-character Z85 set. `activate-snapshot db-instance <string> db-paraphrase <string> [sanity-check-override <true|false>]` puts it back, sanity-check-override default false, pre-condition being that a snapshot must have been taken. `show database-<database-type>` (active, manual, oneday, onehour, oneweek, rollback, temp) lists them with backup-time and description.
